summary: The narrator, alone at night in the rain on a plaza at the ruined site of Baalum, mistakes a bleached jaguar skin with its head still on for a lurking person, then climbs a steep, newly restored pyramid to shelter in a stone hut at its top. Climbing, he reflects that the site may be a fake reconstruction, comparing it to Sir Arthur Evans's reconstruction of the Palace of Minos on Crete, and notes the new-looking wooden lintel above the hut's door. The passage is suspenseful, with the narrator still shaken by the earlier death of Sarah and the threat posed by Ramos.
one_line: Alone in a rainy night at the Mayan site of Baalum, the narrator mistakes a bleached jaguar skin for a threat and climbs a restored pyramid, doubting its authenticity.
key_facts: The narrator sights a white form at the south, forested edge of the plaza at night in the rain and ducks down, fearing someone is waiting to beat him to death as they had Sarah.
The white form turns out to be the skin of a jaguar, bleached white, with the head still on and fearsome teeth bared, hung beside the paved pathway.
The narrator's yellow plastic flashlight beam is swallowed up by the rain.
The narrator thinks his first encounter at Baalum is with a spooky, dead cat, which feels like a chilling omen.
The pyramid appears to have steeper steps than expected but looks like part of a meticulous restoration and brand-new, probably safe to climb.
A stone hut with what appears to be a roof stands at the top of the pyramid.
The narrator wonders whether the pyramid is 'fake'.
Sir Arthur Evans, described as an eccentric Brit archaeologist, 'reconstructed' the Palace of Minos on Crete with his own money about a hundred years earlier.
The Palace of Minos reconstruction is still a tourist highlight, according to the narrator.
The building crowning the pyramid is also a 'restoration', including a decorated wooden lintel above the door that looks newly carved.
The narrator feels the site has the feel of being somebody's crazed obsession.
The narrator fears Ramos may intend to murder him immediately.
The night songs of the birds feel ominous to the narrator, who describes the primeval forest as reasserting its will.
